title: Security+ Study Lab
subtitle: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 practice bank (322 questions)
note: Original practice questions with terminal labs and simulations. Not affiliated with CompTIA. Check the official SY0-701 objectives before you book.

learn.idea: Controls reduce risk. Security+ sorts them two ways: by category (who or what carries them out) and by type (what job they do).
points: Categories: technical (firewalls, encryption), managerial (policies, risk assessments), operational (guards, training, done by people), physical (locks, fences, bollards).

Types: preventive stops an incident, deterrent discourages it, detective finds it, corrective fixes it, compensating stands in when the main control is not possible, directive tells people what to do.
One control can be more than one type. A warning sign is a deterrent and directive. A camera is detective and can deter.
Compensating controls are used when the ideal control cannot be applied, such as isolating a legacy system that cannot be patched.
Defence in depth layers several controls so one failure does not expose everything.
learn.memory: Categories say who does it. Types say what it does.

cards.back: Technical.
Managerial.
Operational (or physical, depending on context).
Detective, and it can deter.
An alternative control used when the main one is not possible.
Corrective control.

questions.q: A company writes a policy that requires annual risk assessments. Which control category is this?
questions.explain: Managerial controls are about planning and oversight, such as policies and risk assessments.

questions.q: A legacy machine cannot be patched, so it is moved to an isolated VLAN with strict ACLs. What type of control is the isolation?
questions.explain: It makes up for the missing patch, which is the control you would normally use.

questions.q: Which control type is an intrusion detection system?
questions.explain: An IDS notices and reports activity. It does not stop it.

questions.q: A 'Restricted area. Authorised staff only.' sign is mainly which control type?
questions.explain: Signs discourage people from trying. They can also be seen as directive.

questions.q: Restoring servers from backups after ransomware is which control type?
questions.explain: Corrective controls repair damage and restore normal operations.

questions.q: Security awareness training delivered by the HR team is which control category?
questions.explain: Operational controls are carried out by people day to day, such as training and guard patrols.

questions.q: Bollards in front of a data centre entrance are which category?
questions.explain: Bollards physically stop vehicles.

questions.q: A firewall rule that blocks inbound Telnet is a technical preventive control.
questions.explain: It is enforced by technology and stops the action before it happens.

questions.q: A control can only ever be one type.
questions.explain: Many controls serve several purposes. Cameras both detect and deter.

questions.q: Match the example to the control type.
questions.explain: Think about what the control does at the moment of the incident.

questions.q: Match the example to the control category.
questions.explain: Category is about how the control is put in place.

learn.idea: The CIA triad, AAA, zero trust and physical security are the foundation the rest of the exam builds on.
points: CIA: confidentiality, integrity, availability. Non-repudiation means a person cannot deny an action, usually through digital signatures.
AAA: authentication, authorisation, accounting. You can authenticate people and systems (for example with device certificates).
Gap analysis compares where you are with where you want to be against a framework.
Zero trust splits into the control plane (adaptive identity, threat scope reduction, policy engine, policy administrator) and the data plane (subject, policy enforcement point).
Physical security: bollards, access control vestibules (mantraps), fencing, lighting, guards, cameras, and sensors (infrared, pressure, microwave, ultrasonic).
Deception and disruption: honeypots, honeynets, honeyfiles and honeytokens lure attackers and raise alerts.
learn.memory: Zero trust: the policy engine decides, the policy administrator tells, the PEP enforces.

cards.back: Proof that someone did something so they cannot deny it.
Comparing current security to a target state.
Zero trust component in the data plane that allows or blocks traffic.
Two doors where only one opens at a time, stopping tailgating.
Fake data, such as a credential, that alerts when used.
Zero trust part that decides whether access is granted.

questions.q: Which zero trust component makes the actual decision to grant or deny access?
questions.explain: The policy engine evaluates the request. The policy administrator passes the decision to the PEP, which enforces it.

questions.q: A digital signature on an email proves the sender cannot later say they did not send it. What does this provide?
questions.explain: Only the sender's private key could make the signature.

questions.q: A small entry room where the second door only opens once the first is closed is used to stop tailgating. What is it?
questions.explain: Vestibules (formerly mantraps) let one person through at a time.

questions.q: A fake AWS key is placed in a code repository. If anyone ever uses it, the security team gets an alert. What is this?
questions.explain: Honeytokens are fake data that should never be used, so any use is a sign of compromise.

questions.q: A company compares its current controls with the CIS Controls to find what is missing. What is this?
questions.explain: Gap analysis shows the difference between current and desired state.

questions.q: Which sensor detects a person by the body heat they give off?
questions.explain: Passive infrared sensors notice heat changes.

questions.q: Servers authenticate to each other using certificates before exchanging data. What is being authenticated?
questions.explain: Authentication applies to systems as well as users.

questions.q: In zero trust, a device on the internal network is trusted by default.
questions.explain: Zero trust removes implicit trust based on location.

questions.q: A honeynet is a network of decoy systems used to study attacker behaviour.
questions.explain: A honeynet is several honeypots set up together.

questions.q: Match the zero trust term to its role.
pairs: Sends the decision and sets up the session
Uses context such as location and device to judge risk
questions.explain: These are named in the SY0-701 objectives.

learn.idea: Uncontrolled changes break systems and open holes. Change management makes sure each change is approved, tested and can be undone.
points: Business processes: approval, ownership, stakeholders, impact analysis, test results, backout plan, maintenance window, standard operating procedure.
Technical effects: allow and deny lists, restricted activities, downtime, service and application restarts, legacy applications, dependencies.
Documentation: update diagrams, policies and procedures after the change. Keep version control for code and configs.
A standard change is pre-approved and low risk. An emergency change follows a faster path but still gets reviewed afterwards.
learn.memory: No owner, no test, no backout plan, no change.

cards.back: Steps to undo a change if it fails.
Agreed time when changes can be made with least impact.
Working out what a change could affect.
Track and roll back changes to code and configs.
Another system or service that relies on what you are changing.
The person or team accountable for it.

questions.q: Before a firewall upgrade, the team writes steps to restore the old firmware if the upgrade fails. What is this?
questions.explain: A backout plan returns systems to the last known good state.

questions.q: A patch to a database server will also restart the web application that depends on it. Which consideration is this?
questions.explain: Dependencies mean one change can affect other systems.

questions.q: Which part of change management sets the time when users will be least affected by downtime?
questions.explain: Changes are scheduled into an agreed window.

questions.q: After a change goes live, which task is often forgotten but required?
questions.explain: Documentation must match the new state or the next responder will be misled.

questions.q: A new application needs a firewall port opened. Which technical implication should be checked in change management?
options: Updating allow lists and deny lists
questions.explain: Allow and deny lists often need changing for new services.

questions.q: Emergency changes skip change management completely.
questions.explain: They move faster but are still recorded and reviewed after the fact.

questions.q: Put the change process in order.
steps: Request the change and name an owner
questions.explain: Request, analyse, test, approve, implement, document.

questions.q: Who should be told about a change that will take the HR system offline for an hour?
options: The stakeholders who use and own it
No one, if it is in the window
questions.explain: Stakeholders need to know so they can plan around downtime.

learn.idea: Cryptography keeps data secret, proves it was not changed and proves who sent it. PKI manages the certificates that tie public keys to identities.
points: Symmetric encryption uses one shared key (AES, ChaCha20). It is fast. Asymmetric uses a public and private key pair (RSA, ECC). It is slower and used for key exchange and signatures.
Hashing (SHA-256, SHA-3) makes a fixed-length digest. It is one way. Salting adds random data before hashing passwords. Key stretching (PBKDF2, bcrypt) slows brute force.
Digital signature: hash the message and encrypt the hash with the sender's private key. Anyone checks it with the public key.
PKI: a certificate authority signs certificates. Root CA, intermediate CA, then leaf certificates. Revocation uses CRLs or OCSP. OCSP stapling lets the server attach the status.
Certificate types: wildcard (*.example.com), SAN (many names), self-signed, code signing.
Encryption levels: full disk, partition, volume, file, database, record. Transport encryption with TLS. Key storage in a TPM, HSM or key management service.
Other tools: tokenisation, data masking, steganography, blockchain and open public ledgers.
learn.memory: Encrypt with their public key so only they can read it. Sign with your private key so everyone can check it.

cards.back: AES.
RSA or ECC.
Makes identical passwords hash differently and defeats rainbow tables.
Online check of whether a certificate is revoked.
Covers all subdomains at one level, such as *.example.com.
Dedicated hardware that stores and uses keys securely.

questions.q: Alice wants to send Bob a file that only Bob can decrypt. Which key does she encrypt it with?
questions.explain: Only Bob's private key can decrypt data encrypted with his public key.

questions.q: Which key is used to create a digital signature?
questions.explain: Signing uses the private key. Anyone with the public key can verify.

questions.q: Which algorithm is a symmetric block cipher?
questions.explain: AES uses the same key to encrypt and decrypt.

questions.q: Why are random salts added to passwords before hashing?
options: So identical passwords produce different hashes and rainbow tables fail
To encrypt the password with AES
questions.explain: A unique salt per account means attackers must crack each hash on its own.

questions.q: A browser needs to check quickly whether a site's certificate has been revoked. Which protocol is used?
questions.explain: Online Certificate Status Protocol returns the status of one certificate. Stapling lets the server send it.

questions.q: One certificate must cover www.example.com, mail.example.com and shop.example.org. Which type fits?
questions.explain: Subject Alternative Name lists several names, even across domains. A wildcard only covers one domain level.

questions.q: Which hardware chip on a laptop stores keys used for BitLocker full disk encryption?
questions.explain: The Trusted Platform Module stores keys and checks boot integrity.

questions.q: A payment system replaces card numbers with random values and keeps the mapping in a secure vault. What is this?
questions.explain: Tokens have no value if stolen. The vault maps them back.

questions.q: Which technique hides data inside an image file?
questions.explain: Steganography conceals data inside other files such as images or audio.

questions.q: Which technique slows down password cracking by running the hash many thousands of times?
questions.explain: PBKDF2, bcrypt and Argon2 make each guess expensive.

questions.q: Which protocol lets two parties agree on a shared secret over an untrusted network without sending the secret?
questions.explain: Diffie-Hellman key exchange creates a shared key from public values. ECDHE is the elliptic curve version.

questions.q: A hash can be decrypted back to the original data if you have the right key.
questions.explain: Hashing is one way. There is no key to reverse it.

questions.q: Asymmetric encryption is usually used to exchange a symmetric session key, which then encrypts the bulk data.
questions.explain: TLS does this because symmetric ciphers are much faster.

questions.q: Match the item to its use.
questions.explain: Pick the algorithm by the job.

questions.q: Match the PKI term to its meaning.
pairs: Request sent to a CA to get a certificate
Signed by its own key, not a trusted CA
questions.explain: These terms come up in certificate questions.

questions.q: A company stores encryption keys in a dedicated, tamper-resistant appliance that does the crypto operations itself. What is it?
questions.explain: A hardware security module protects keys for servers and CAs.

questions.q: A developer needs test data that looks real but must not expose customer names. Which method fits?
questions.explain: Masking replaces real values with realistic fake ones.

questions.q: A user trusts a site whose certificate was signed by an intermediate CA. What must the browser also trust?
options: The root CA at the top of the chain
questions.explain: Trust flows down from a root CA in the browser's store through the intermediate to the site's certificate.

questions.q: Which type of encryption protects one database column such as social security numbers, while the rest of the table stays readable?
questions.explain: Granular encryption targets only sensitive fields.

questions.q: Which statement about ECC compared to RSA is correct?
options: ECC gives the same strength with much shorter keys
ECC cannot be used for signatures
ECC needs longer keys than RSA
questions.explain: A 256-bit ECC key is about as strong as a 3072-bit RSA key, which suits phones and IoT.

learn.idea: Knowing who attacks and why helps you guess how they will attack and how hard they will try.
points: Nation-state: well funded, patient, often behind advanced persistent threats (APTs). Motivated by espionage, war or disruption.
Organised crime: money first, using ransomware, fraud and data theft.
Hacktivist: driven by a cause or belief. Defacement, leaks, DDoS.
Insider threat: a current or former employee or contractor with access. Can be malicious or careless.
Unskilled attacker (script kiddie): uses tools made by others. Low sophistication.
Shadow IT: staff using unapproved systems, which creates hidden risk.

Attributes: internal or external, resources and funding, level of sophistication. Motivations: data exfiltration, espionage, service disruption, blackmail, financial gain, philosophical or political beliefs, ethical, revenge, chaos, war.
learn.memory: Follow the money for crime, the flag for nations and the cause for hacktivists.

cards.back: Advanced persistent threat, usually a nation-state.
Political or social cause.
Unapproved IT used by staff.

cards.front: Most likely to use ransomware for profit?
cards.back: Organised crime.
Someone with authorised access who causes harm.
Uses existing tools with little skill.

questions.q: A group stays hidden inside a defence contractor's network for two years, quietly copying designs. Which actor is most likely?
questions.explain: Long, stealthy espionage with heavy resources points to a nation-state APT.

questions.q: A group defaces a government web site with a political message. Which actor is most likely?
questions.explain: Hacktivists attack to promote a cause.

questions.q: A marketing team signs up for an unapproved cloud file sharing service and uploads client files. What is this?
questions.explain: Shadow IT is technology used without IT's approval or oversight.

questions.q: A fired employee uses an account that was never disabled to delete files. Which actor is this?
questions.explain: Former staff with leftover access are insider threats.

questions.q: Which actor is most likely to deploy ransomware and demand payment in cryptocurrency?
questions.explain: Financial gain is the main driver for criminal groups.

questions.q: A teenager runs a downloaded DDoS tool against a game server. Which actor is this?
questions.explain: Unskilled attackers use tools other people wrote.

questions.q: Which attribute best separates a nation-state from an unskilled attacker?
questions.explain: Nation-states have big budgets, custom tools and patience.

questions.q: An insider threat is always malicious.
questions.explain: Careless insiders who click phishing links or misconfigure systems are also insider threats.

questions.q: Espionage is a common motivation for nation-state actors.
questions.explain: Stealing government, military or industrial secrets is a key goal.

questions.q: Match the actor to its usual motivation.
questions.explain: Motivation helps predict targets and methods.

questions.q: A competitor hires someone to steal a rival's product roadmap. Which motivation is this?
questions.explain: Corporate espionage steals secrets for advantage.

questions.q: Which actor is classed as internal?
options: A contractor with a company laptop and VPN access
questions.explain: Anyone with authorised access through the organisation is internal.

learn.idea: A threat vector is the path an attacker uses to get in. People are often the easiest path, which is why social engineering is so common.
points: Message-based: email, SMS (smishing), instant messages. Also image-based and file-based attacks, voice calls (vishing) and removable devices.
Vulnerable software: client-based or agentless. Unsupported systems and apps. Unsecured networks: wireless, wired, Bluetooth.
Open service ports and default credentials are easy wins for attackers.
Supply chain: managed service providers, vendors and suppliers can be the way in.
Social engineering: phishing, vishing, smishing, misinformation and disinformation, impersonation, business email compromise, pretexting, watering hole, brand impersonation, typosquatting.
Principles attackers use: authority, urgency, scarcity, familiarity, social proof, intimidation.
learn.memory: Smishing is SMS. Vishing is voice. Whaling hunts the big fish.

cards.back: Phishing by SMS text.
Phishing by voice call.
Infecting a site the target group visits.
Registering misspelled domains like gooogle.com.
Inventing a believable story to get information.
Using a real or spoofed executive mailbox to trick staff into paying or sharing.

questions.q: Staff get a text saying their parcel is held and they must pay a small fee at a link. What attack is this?
questions.explain: Phishing over SMS is smishing.

questions.q: An attacker compromises a trade association site that engineers at the target company visit every day. What is this?
questions.explain: Watering hole attacks infect a site the victims trust and visit.

questions.q: Someone registers micros0ft-support.com to catch users who mistype the address. What is this?
questions.explain: Typosquatting relies on users mistyping a URL.

questions.q: An attacker calls the help desk pretending to be a regional manager stuck at an airport who needs a password reset right away. Which two principles are used?
questions.explain: Claiming to be a manager uses authority. Needing it right now uses urgency.

questions.q: The finance team gets an email from the CFO's real account asking for an urgent wire transfer to a new supplier. The CFO's mailbox had been taken over. What is this?
questions.explain: BEC uses a compromised or spoofed executive mailbox to commit fraud.

questions.q: USB drives labelled 'Salaries 2026' are left in the car park. Which threat vector is this?
questions.explain: Baiting with removable media relies on curiosity.

questions.q: Attackers break into a managed service provider and use its remote tools to reach the MSP's customers. What is this?
questions.explain: The trusted provider becomes the way in.

questions.q: A caller says they are from the bank's fraud team and asks the victim to read out a one-time code. What is this?
questions.explain: Voice phishing uses phone calls.

questions.q: A fake news story spread on purpose to damage a company's share price is an example of what?
questions.explain: Disinformation is false on purpose. Misinformation is false but shared without intent to deceive.

questions.q: An attacker scans the internet for devices still using admin/admin. Which vector is this?
questions.explain: Default credentials are published in manuals and are easy to try.

questions.q: Phishing that targets one specific person using researched details is called spear phishing.
questions.explain: Spear phishing is tailored. Whaling is spear phishing aimed at senior executives.

questions.q: An unsupported operating system is not a threat vector if it is behind a firewall.
questions.explain: Unsupported systems get no patches. Attackers who reach them, for example through phishing, can exploit known flaws.

questions.q: Match the attack to its description.
pairs: A made-up story to gain trust
Fake emails or sites copying a known company
Watching someone type a PIN or password
questions.explain: Social engineering questions often test these definitions.

questions.q: Match the principle to the example.
pairs: Everyone in your team has already signed up
Do this now or you will be reported
Hi, it's Dave from IT again
questions.explain: Attackers combine these to rush people past their judgement.

questions.q: A new hire gets a Microsoft Teams message from 'IT Support' asking them to install a remote access tool. Which vector is this?
questions.explain: Message-based vectors include chat apps as well as email and SMS.

questions.q: Which control best reduces the success of phishing emails across the company?
options: Security awareness training with phishing simulations
Adding more RAM to the mail server
questions.explain: Trained users report and ignore phishing. Email filtering helps too.

learn.idea: A vulnerability is a weakness an attacker can use. Security+ lists vulnerabilities in applications, operating systems, hardware, cloud, mobile and the supply chain.
points: Application: memory injection, buffer overflow, race conditions (time-of-check to time-of-use), malicious updates.
Web: SQL injection (SQLi), cross-site scripting (XSS), cross-site request forgery (CSRF), directory traversal, server-side request forgery (SSRF).
OS-based flaws, missing patches, firmware flaws, end-of-life hardware and legacy systems.
Virtualisation: VM escape, resource reuse. Cloud: misconfigured storage, weak identity settings.
Mobile: side loading, jailbreaking or rooting.
Zero-day: a flaw the vendor does not know about or has not fixed yet.
Cryptographic weaknesses and misconfiguration are among the most common real-world problems.
learn.memory: Input you did not check is input the attacker controls.

cards.back: Injecting SQL through input to read or change a database.
Injecting script that runs in other users' browsers.
Writing past a memory buffer to crash or run code.
Breaking out of a VM to reach the host or other VMs.
Unknown or unpatched vulnerability.
Race condition between checking and using a resource.

questions.q: A login form accepts ' OR 1=1 -- as the username and logs the attacker in. What vulnerability is this?
questions.explain: The input changed the SQL query. Parameterised queries fix this.

questions.q: A forum lets users post <script> tags that run in other visitors' browsers and steal their session cookies. What is this?
questions.explain: Stored XSS saves the script on the server so every viewer runs it. Output encoding prevents it.

questions.q: A request for /download?file=../../../../etc/passwd returns the server's password file. What vulnerability is this?
questions.explain: The ../ sequences climb out of the intended folder.

questions.q: A program copies user input into a fixed 64-byte buffer without checking length, letting an attacker overwrite the return address. What is this?
questions.explain: Writing beyond a buffer can crash the program or let attackers run code. Bounds checking and memory-safe languages help.

questions.q: A user who is logged in to their bank visits a malicious page that silently submits a money transfer form to the bank. What is this?
questions.explain: CSRF abuses the browser's existing session. Anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies stop it.

questions.q: Attackers exploit a flaw in a VPN appliance before the vendor has released a patch. What is this?
questions.explain: No fix exists yet, so detection and compensating controls are needed.

questions.q: A web app fetches any URL a user gives it. An attacker makes it request the cloud metadata service at 169.254.169.254 and steals credentials. What is this?
questions.explain: SSRF makes the server send requests on the attacker's behalf, often to internal resources.

questions.q: Malware running in a guest VM breaks out and runs code on the hypervisor. What is this?
questions.explain: VM escape breaks the isolation between guests and host.

questions.q: A user installs apps on a work phone from a website instead of the official store. What is this called?
questions.explain: Side loaded apps skip store vetting and may carry malware.

questions.q: A program checks a file's permissions, then opens it a moment later. An attacker swaps the file in between. What is this?
questions.explain: Time-of-check to time-of-use flaws exploit the gap between the check and the action.

questions.q: A cloud storage bucket holding customer records was set to public read. What kind of vulnerability is this?
questions.explain: Misconfigured cloud resources are among the most common causes of breaches.

questions.q: Attackers compromise a software vendor's build server and ship a backdoor inside a signed update. What is this?
questions.explain: Users trust signed updates, which makes this very effective. SolarWinds is a well-known example.

questions.q: Jailbreaking an iPhone removes some of the operating system's built-in security restrictions.
questions.explain: Jailbreaking (iOS) and rooting (Android) bypass the vendor's controls.

questions.q: Legacy systems are safe as long as they still work.
questions.explain: End-of-life systems get no security patches, so known flaws stay open.

questions.q: Match the vulnerability to the best fix.
questions.explain: Secure coding fixes each class of bug at its root.

questions.q: Which statement describes memory injection?
options: Malicious code is placed into the memory of a running process
Data is written to a USB drive
An update file is replaced on disk
questions.explain: Attackers inject code into another process's memory to run it with that process's rights and avoid detection.

learn.idea: Attacks leave traces. Security+ expects you to read the clues and name the attack, from malware to password attacks to network abuse.
points: Malware: ransomware, trojan, worm, spyware, bloatware, virus, keylogger, logic bomb, rootkit.
Network attacks: DDoS (amplified, reflected), DNS attacks, wireless, on-path, credential replay, malicious code.
Application attacks: injection, buffer overflow, replay, privilege escalation, forgery, directory traversal.
Password attacks: spraying (one common password against many accounts) and brute force (many passwords against one account).
Cryptographic attacks: downgrade, collision, birthday.

Indicators: account lockouts, concurrent session use, blocked content, impossible travel, resource consumption, resource inaccessibility, out-of-cycle logging, published or documented attacks, missing logs.
learn.memory: Spraying is one password, many users. Brute force is many passwords, one user.

cards.back: Malicious code that runs when a condition is met.
Malware that hides deep in the OS to keep access.
Logins from far apart places too close in time.
One common password tried against many accounts.
Forcing a weaker protocol or cipher.
Finding hash collisions faster than brute force.

questions.q: Malware spreads from PC to PC on its own using an SMB flaw with no user action. What is it?
questions.explain: Worms self-propagate across networks.

questions.q: Free software a user installed also quietly opened a remote access backdoor. What type of malware is this?
questions.explain: A trojan pretends to be useful software while doing something harmful.

questions.explain: Replay attacks reuse captured traffic. Timestamps, nonces and session tokens defeat them.

questions.q: An attacker on the network forces a client and server to agree on an old, weak TLS version. What is this?
questions.explain: Downgrade attacks push connections to weaker protocols that can be broken.

questions.q: Logs on a file server stop for six hours overnight, then start again. What does this most likely indicate?
options: Missing logs, possibly from an attacker covering tracks
questions.explain: Gaps in logging are an indicator that someone may have tampered with records.

questions.q: A standard user account suddenly has domain admin rights with no change ticket. What attack is indicated?
questions.explain: Gaining rights beyond what was granted is privilege escalation.

questions.q: Malware hides its files and processes from Task Manager and antivirus by changing the kernel. What is it?
questions.explain: Rootkits hide in the OS or firmware to keep stealthy access.

questions.q: A single account locked out after hundreds of attempts with different passwords is a sign of a brute force attack.
questions.explain: Many passwords against one account is brute force.

questions.q: Match the malware to its behaviour.
pairs: Attaches to files and needs user action to spread
questions.explain: Behaviour is how you identify malware on the exam.

questions.q: Attackers send small spoofed requests to open NTP servers, which flood the victim with large replies. What is this?
questions.explain: Reflection hides the source and amplification multiplies the traffic.

learn.idea: Once you know the threats, you reduce them. These techniques come up again and again in scenario questions.
points: Segmentation limits how far an attacker can move. Access control lists and permissions limit who reaches what.
Application allow lists only let approved programs run. Isolation and sandboxing contain risky code.
Patching closes known holes. Encryption protects data even if stolen. Monitoring finds what slips through.
Least privilege and configuration enforcement keep systems in a known good state.
Decommissioning removes old systems safely. Hardening: disable unused ports and services, change defaults, remove unneeded software, install endpoint protection and host firewalls, use HIPS.
learn.memory: Patch it, segment it, least-privilege it, watch it.

cards.back: Only approved software can run.
Limits lateral movement.
Host-based intrusion prevention system.
Retiring systems safely, including wiping data.
Separating a system so it cannot affect others.
Keeping systems at an approved baseline.

questions.q: Ransomware keeps running from users' Downloads folders. Which control stops unknown executables from running at all?
questions.explain: An allow list only lets approved programs run.

questions.q: An attacker who took over a reception PC cannot reach the database servers because they are in a different zone with strict rules. Which mitigation worked?
questions.explain: Segmentation contains the attacker.

questions.q: An infected laptop is moved to a quarantine VLAN with no access while it is investigated. What is this?
questions.explain: Isolation stops it spreading while evidence is kept.

questions.q: Which step should come before recycling old servers?
options: Securely wipe or destroy the drives as part of decommissioning
questions.explain: Decommissioning must remove sensitive data.

questions.q: Disabling unused services and ports is a hardening technique.
questions.explain: Every running service is a possible way in. Turn off what you do not need.

questions.q: Match the mitigation to the threat it best addresses.
questions.explain: Pick the control that breaks the attack path.

questions.q: A host has a firewall, antivirus with EDR, and an intrusion prevention agent. What is the agent called?
questions.explain: A host-based intrusion prevention system blocks attacks on the endpoint.

questions.q: A suspicious email attachment is opened in a safe, throwaway environment to watch what it does. What is this?
questions.explain: A sandbox lets code run without touching real systems.

learn.idea: Where and how a system runs changes its risks. Cloud, containers, IoT and industrial systems each bring their own security trade-offs.
points: Shared responsibility: the cloud provider secures the cloud itself, the customer secures what they put in it. The customer's share grows from SaaS to PaaS to IaaS.
Infrastructure as code (IaC) defines systems in templates, so builds are repeatable and can be scanned before deployment.
Serverless runs functions without managing servers. Microservices split an app into small services that talk over APIs.
Containers share the host OS kernel and are lighter than VMs. VMs each have their own OS on a hypervisor.
Air-gapped networks have no connection to other networks. Logical segmentation uses VLANs and software-defined networking.
ICS and SCADA control physical processes such as power and water. They value availability and often run old, hard-to-patch systems.
Embedded systems and RTOS (real-time OS) run devices like medical pumps and car controllers. IoT devices are often cheap and poorly secured.
learn.memory: You always own your data, your identities and your configuration, whatever the cloud model.

cards.back: Provider secures the cloud, customer secures what is in it.
Infrastructure defined in code templates.
Containers share the host kernel. VMs have full OSs.
Supervisory control and data acquisition for industrial processes.
Physically separate network with no connections.
Real-time OS for devices that must respond within strict time limits.

questions.q: Under the shared responsibility model for IaaS, who patches the guest operating system?
questions.explain: In IaaS the provider secures hardware and the hypervisor. The customer manages the OS and up.

questions.q: A team defines all cloud networks and servers in Terraform files stored in Git. What is this practice?
questions.explain: IaC makes builds repeatable and lets templates be reviewed and scanned.

questions.q: A water treatment plant's pump controllers run on a network with no connection to the corporate LAN or internet. What is this?
questions.explain: An air gap physically separates the network.

questions.q: Which is the biggest security concern with many ICS and SCADA systems?
options: They run legacy software that is hard to patch without downtime
They only run in the cloud
questions.explain: ICS puts availability first and often runs old systems, so compensating controls such as segmentation are used.

questions.q: An app is split into small independent services that each do one job and talk over APIs. What is this?
questions.explain: Microservices can be scaled and updated separately, but every API is something to secure.

questions.q: What is the key security difference between containers and virtual machines?
options: Containers share the host kernel, so a kernel flaw can affect all of them
Containers each have their own kernel
questions.explain: Shared kernels make containers light but reduce isolation compared to VMs.

questions.q: Developers deploy code as functions that run only when triggered, and the provider handles all servers. What is this?
questions.explain: Serverless (function as a service) removes server management from the customer.

questions.q: Smart light bulbs on the office Wi-Fi use default passwords and never get updates. What is the best mitigation?
options: Put IoT devices on a separate segmented network
questions.explain: Segmentation stops a compromised IoT device from reaching important systems.

questions.q: Moving to SaaS means the customer no longer has any security responsibility.
questions.explain: The customer still manages users, access, data and configuration settings.

questions.q: A real-time operating system must respond to events within strict time limits.
questions.explain: RTOSs run things like car brakes and industrial robots where delays are dangerous.

questions.q: Match the cloud model to what the customer manages.
questions.explain: Customer responsibility grows as you move down the stack.

questions.q: Which is a benefit of centralised architecture over decentralised?
options: Easier to monitor and control from one place
questions.explain: Central control simplifies management but can create a single point of failure.

questions.q: A hospital's infusion pumps run a fixed embedded OS from the vendor. Which issue is most likely?
options: Patches depend on the vendor and are slow or unavailable
questions.explain: Embedded devices rely on vendor updates and are often isolated as a compensating control.

questions.q: Which cloud concern is about the legal rules that apply based on the country where data is physically stored?
questions.explain: Data in a country falls under that country's laws.

learn.idea: Good architecture places security devices in the right zones and chooses how they behave when they fail.
points: Security zones separate trusted, untrusted and screened areas. Reduce the attack surface by removing what is not needed.
Fail-open keeps traffic flowing if the device fails (availability). Fail-closed blocks traffic (security).
Active devices act on traffic (IPS). Passive devices watch a copy (IDS on a tap or SPAN). Inline devices sit in the path.
Appliances: jump server, proxy, IPS/IDS, load balancer, sensors. Firewalls: WAF (web apps, Layer 7), UTM (all-in-one), NGFW (application aware), Layer 4 and Layer 7.
Port security and 802.1X with EAP control who plugs in.
Secure communication: VPN, remote access, tunnelling with IPsec and TLS, SD-WAN, SASE (secure access service edge, which combines SD-WAN and cloud security services).
learn.memory: Fail-open favours uptime. Fail-closed favours security.

cards.back: Blocks all traffic when the device fails.
Firewall that protects web applications at Layer 7.
All-in-one firewall, IPS, antivirus and filtering appliance.
Cloud-delivered networking and security combined, including SD-WAN, SWG, CASB and ZTNA.
Watching a copy of traffic without being able to block it.
All the points an attacker could try to use.

questions.q: A firewall protecting a bank's payment systems should block everything if it crashes. Which failure mode is this?
questions.explain: Fail-closed protects security at the cost of availability.

questions.q: Which device inspects HTTP requests to block SQL injection and XSS against a web app?
questions.explain: A web application firewall understands web traffic and its attacks.

questions.q: An IDS is connected to a network tap. Which description fits?
questions.explain: On a tap it only sees a copy and cannot block traffic.

questions.q: A small business wants one box that does firewalling, IPS, antivirus scanning and web filtering. What should it buy?
questions.explain: Unified threat management bundles many functions in one device.

questions.q: Remote staff and branches connect through a cloud service that combines SD-WAN, secure web gateway, CASB and zero trust access. What is this?
questions.explain: Secure access service edge delivers network and security services from the cloud.

questions.q: Admins must connect to a hardened host in the management zone before reaching servers. What is that host?
questions.explain: A jump server is a single controlled entry point for admin access.

questions.q: An IPS sits in the traffic path for an e-commerce site that must never go offline. If the IPS fails, traffic should keep flowing. Which mode is chosen?
questions.explain: Fail-open keeps the business running, accepting less protection during the fault.

questions.q: Which firewall type makes decisions based only on IPs, ports and protocol?
questions.explain: Layer 4 firewalls do not look inside application payloads.

questions.q: Which 802.1X component carries authentication messages between the supplicant and the RADIUS server?
questions.explain: 802.1X uses EAP. The switch or AP relays EAP between client and server.

questions.q: Removing unused services and software reduces the attack surface.
questions.explain: Fewer exposed components means fewer ways in.

questions.q: A reverse proxy sits in front of internal clients to make internet requests for them.
questions.explain: That is a forward proxy. A reverse proxy sits in front of servers.

questions.q: Match the device to its job.
pairs: Makes web requests for users and can filter them
Collects traffic or events for analysis
Firewall that identifies applications and users
questions.explain: Placement and purpose questions are common in this domain.

questions.q: Which secure tunnelling protocol is used by most site-to-site VPNs between firewalls?
questions.explain: IPsec protects traffic between gateways at Layer 3.

questions.q: A company wants to cut costs by using broadband links at branches with central policy and failover, replacing MPLS. What fits?
questions.explain: SD-WAN manages many links centrally and can encrypt the overlay.

questions.q: Where should a public-facing web server be placed?
options: In a screened subnet between two firewalls
In the same VLAN as the domain controllers
questions.explain: The screened subnet (DMZ) keeps public systems apart from the internal network.

questions.q: Which control limits a switch port to the specific device MAC addresses allowed to use it?
questions.explain: Port security restricts and can shut down ports on unknown MACs.

learn.idea: Data protection starts with knowing what data you have, how sensitive it is and where it lives. The method you use depends on the state of the data.
points: Data types: regulated (health, payment card, personal data), trade secret, intellectual property, legal, financial, human and non-human readable.
Classifications: sensitive, confidential, public, restricted, private, critical.
Data states: at rest (stored), in transit (moving), in use (being processed in memory).
Data sovereignty and geolocation: data is subject to the laws of where it is stored and processed.
Methods: geographic restrictions, encryption, hashing, masking, tokenisation, obfuscation, segmentation, permission restrictions.
learn.memory: At rest, in transit, in use: three states, three kinds of protection.

cards.back: Data being processed in memory.
Health records or card data.
Data falls under the laws of where it is stored.
Limiting access or storage to certain regions.
Making data or code hard to understand.
Confidential business information that gives an advantage.

questions.q: Card numbers are being processed by an app in RAM. Which data state is this?
questions.explain: Data being worked on in memory is in use.

questions.q: Files are copied between offices over a VPN. Which data state is protected by the VPN?
questions.explain: Encryption on the wire protects data in transit.

questions.q: An EU company must keep customer records in EU data centres. Which concept drives this?
questions.explain: Laws such as GDPR apply based on where data is stored and processed.

questions.q: A cloud storage policy blocks access from any country where the company does not operate. What is this?
questions.explain: Geofencing access cuts exposure from unexpected regions.

questions.q: A soft drink recipe that the company keeps secret is which data type?
questions.explain: Trade secrets are valuable because they stay secret.

questions.q: Patient records are which data type?
questions.explain: Health data is regulated by laws such as HIPAA.

questions.q: Only the HR group can open the salary folder. Which method is this?
questions.explain: Access permissions limit who can read data.

questions.q: Encrypting a laptop's drive protects the data while it is being processed in memory.
questions.explain: Full disk encryption protects data at rest. Data in use is decrypted in memory.

questions.q: A barcode is an example of non-human readable data.
questions.explain: It needs a machine to interpret it.

questions.q: Match the data state to the protection.
questions.explain: Each state needs a different control.

questions.q: Match the classification to an example.
pairs: Merger plans for a few executives
Data needed to keep the business running
questions.explain: Labels set who can see data and how it is handled.

questions.q: Which method replaces sensitive data with a random value, keeping the real value in a secure vault?
questions.explain: Tokens can be mapped back only through the vault.

learn.idea: Resilience keeps the business running through failures and disasters. It covers redundant systems, backups, power and testing.
points: High availability uses load balancing (spreading work) or clustering (servers acting as one, with failover).
Site considerations: hot, warm and cold sites. Geographic dispersion keeps one disaster from taking out every site.
Platform diversity and multi-cloud avoid relying on one vendor. Continuity of operations (COOP) keeps essential functions running.
Capacity planning covers people, technology and infrastructure.
Testing: tabletop exercises, failover, simulation, parallel processing.
Backups: onsite and offsite, frequency, encryption, snapshots, recovery testing, replication, journaling.
Power: UPS for short outages and generators for long ones.
learn.memory: A backup you never restored is a backup you hope works.

cards.back: Several servers working as one with failover.
Spreading sites so one disaster cannot hit them all.
Point-in-time copy of a system or volume.
Logging changes so data can be replayed to a point in time.
Running the backup site alongside production to compare.
Continuity of operations planning.

questions.q: Two database servers share storage and one takes over automatically if the other fails. What is this?
questions.explain: A failover cluster presents one service across several nodes.

questions.q: A company keeps its backup data centre 800 km away from headquarters. Which principle is this?
questions.explain: Distance protects against regional disasters such as hurricanes.

questions.q: The DR team runs the backup site alongside production on real data to compare results without cutting over. What test is this?
questions.explain: Parallel tests prove the backup site works without risking production.

questions.q: A company uses both AWS and Azure for key services so one provider's outage will not stop the business. What is this?
questions.explain: Multi-cloud reduces dependence on a single provider.

questions.q: Which backup approach copies data to another site continuously so it is almost up to date?
questions.explain: Replication keeps a second copy in near real time. It also copies corruption, so it does not replace backups.

questions.q: A hypervisor saves the state of a VM at 2 pm so it can be rolled back if an update fails. What is this?
questions.explain: Snapshots capture a point in time.

questions.q: Ransomware encrypted the backups on the same network as the servers. Which practice would have helped most?
options: Offsite or offline, immutable backup copies
More frequent snapshots on the same storage
questions.explain: Keeping a copy offline or immutable stops attackers from reaching it.

questions.q: Which power device keeps servers running for a few minutes during an outage until the generator starts?
questions.explain: The UPS bridges the gap with batteries.

questions.q: Backups should be tested by actually restoring data.
questions.explain: Restores prove backups are complete and usable.

questions.q: Load balancing and clustering are exactly the same thing.
questions.explain: Load balancing spreads work among servers. Clustering joins servers to act as one, often for failover.

questions.q: Match the resilience term to its meaning.
pairs: Ready to take over almost immediately
Has equipment but needs data and setup
Using different vendors or systems to avoid one shared flaw
questions.explain: Site types trade cost against recovery speed.

questions.q: Planning how many staff, servers and bandwidth the business will need next year is called what?
questions.explain: Capacity planning covers people, technology and infrastructure.

questions.q: Backups are encrypted before they are sent to the cloud. Which risk does this address?
options: Exposure of backup data if the storage is breached
questions.explain: Encrypted backups stay confidential even if someone gets the files.

learn.idea: Secure baselines and hardening make each system harder to attack. Mobile devices and applications need their own controls.
points: Secure baselines: establish, deploy and maintain them. CIS Benchmarks and vendor guides are common starting points.
Hardening targets: mobile devices, workstations, switches, routers, cloud infrastructure, servers, ICS/SCADA, embedded systems, RTOS, IoT.
Wireless: site surveys and heat maps, WPA3, AAA with RADIUS, EAP methods.
Mobile: MDM, deployment models BYOD (bring your own), COPE (corporate owned, personally enabled), CYOD (choose your own). Connection methods: cellular, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth.
Application security: input validation, secure cookies (Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite), static code analysis, code signing, sandboxing.
Monitoring confirms hardening stays in place.
learn.memory: Baseline it, harden it, then check it never drifts.

Central management of mobile devices.

questions.q: A company buys phones for staff and lets them install personal apps, while MDM keeps work data in a separate container. Which deployment model is this?

questions.explain: SAST tools scan source code without running it.

questions.q: In BYOD the company owns the device.

questions.q: Match the mobile deployment model to its meaning.

learn.idea: You cannot protect what you do not know you have. Asset management tracks every device and data store from purchase to disposal.

Assignment and accounting: ownership and classification for each asset.
Monitoring and tracking: inventory and enumeration.
Disposal: sanitisation (wiping or degaussing), destruction (shredding, pulverising, incineration), certification of destruction, and data retention rules.

Discovering and listing assets.

Keeping data for a required time, then disposing of it.

learn.idea: Vulnerability management is a loop: find weaknesses, rank them, fix them, check the fix and report.
points: Identification: vulnerability scans, SAST and DAST, package monitoring, threat feeds (OSINT, paid, ISACs, dark web), penetration tests, responsible disclosure and bug bounties, audits.
Analysis: confirm results (false positives and false negatives), prioritise with CVSS scores and CVE IDs, and weigh exposure factor, environment and risk tolerance.
Response: patch, buy insurance, segment, use compensating controls, or grant documented exceptions.
Validation: rescan, audit and verify the fix worked. Then report.

learn.memory: False positive: alarm with no fire. False negative: fire with no alarm.

Percentage of an asset's value lost if exploited

learn.idea: Security operations watch everything and tune tools so real threats stand out. Email, DNS, web and endpoint controls all feed the picture.
points: Activities: log aggregation, alerting, scanning, reporting, archiving, alert response and remediation, quarantine and alert tuning.
Tools: SCAP, benchmarks, agents and agentless, SIEM, antivirus, DLP, SNMP traps, NetFlow, vulnerability scanners.
Web filtering: agent-based or central proxy, URL scanning, content categories, block rules, reputation.
DNS filtering blocks known bad domains. Email security uses SPF (allowed senders), DKIM (signature) and DMARC (policy and reporting) plus a secure email gateway.
File integrity monitoring (FIM) alerts when key files change. DLP stops sensitive data leaving.
EDR watches endpoints for suspicious behaviour and can respond. XDR combines endpoint, network, cloud and email data. User behaviour analytics (UBA) spots unusual user activity.
OS security: Group Policy for Windows, SELinux for Linux mandatory access control.
learn.memory: SPF says who may send, DKIM proves it was signed, DMARC says what to do when they fail.

Digital signature on email headers and body.
Policy telling receivers what to do with mail that fails SPF or DKIM.
Alerts on changes to important files.
Endpoint detection and response.
Linux mandatory access control system.

questions.q: Which tool combines detection data from endpoints, network, cloud and email into one view with automated response?
questions.explain: Extended detection and response joins many sources.

questions.q: An account that normally works 9 to 5 suddenly downloads 30 GB at 3 am. Which tool is designed to notice this?
questions.explain: UBA builds a baseline for each user and flags unusual actions.

questions.explain: Security Content Automation Protocol supports automated compliance checks.

questions.explain: Agentless tools collect data remotely, for example over WMI or SSH. Agent-based tools install software.

questions.explain: Each enterprise tool fills a gap.

learn.idea: IAM decides who someone is and what they can reach. Strong identity controls stop most account takeovers.
points: Provisioning and deprovisioning accounts. Identity proofing checks who someone is before creating an account.
Federation lets one organisation trust another's identities. SSO uses LDAP, OAuth (authorisation), OpenID Connect and SAML (authentication assertions).
Access models: mandatory (labels), discretionary (owner decides), role-based, rule-based, attribute-based (ABAC), time-of-day restrictions, least privilege.
MFA: biometrics, hard tokens, soft tokens, security keys (FIDO2). Factors: know, have, are, somewhere you are.
Passwords: length beats complexity. Avoid reuse. Password managers help. Passwordless uses keys or biometrics.
Privileged access management (PAM): just-in-time permissions, password vaulting, ephemeral credentials.
Attestation: managers regularly confirm their staff still need their access.
learn.memory: SAML says who you are. OAuth says what an app may do for you.

cards.back: XML-based standard for exchanging authentication between an IdP and service.
Authorisation framework that grants apps limited access with tokens.
Access based on attributes such as department, location and device.
Privileges given only when needed and removed after.
Trusting identities from another organisation.
Regular review that access is still needed.

questions.q: Employees log in once and reach Salesforce, Workday and Microsoft 365 without logging in again. Which technology is this?
questions.explain: SSO with SAML passes signed assertions from the identity provider to each app.

questions.q: A user lets a calendar app read their Google contacts without giving it their password. Which standard is used?
questions.explain: OAuth grants scoped access tokens for authorisation.

questions.q: Access is granted only if the user is in Finance, on a managed device, and in Jamaica. Which access model is this?
questions.explain: ABAC combines attributes of the user, resource and environment.

questions.q: A military system uses labels such as Secret and Top Secret that users cannot change. Which model is this?
questions.explain: MAC enforces labels set by the system and administrators.

questions.q: The owner of a file share decides who can read it. Which model is this?
questions.explain: In DAC the owner controls permissions, as in NTFS.

questions.q: Admins request domain admin rights for two hours when needed, and the rights are removed automatically. What is this?
questions.explain: JIT access shrinks the window when powerful rights exist.

questions.q: Which MFA method best resists phishing?
questions.explain: FIDO2 keys check the site's origin, so they do not work on fake sites.

questions.q: Managers must confirm every quarter that their team members still need their system access. What is this?
questions.explain: Regular attestation finds and removes access creep.

questions.q: Two companies merge and want staff from each to use the other's apps with their existing accounts. What should they set up?
questions.explain: Federation lets each organisation trust the other's identity provider.

questions.q: A help desk verifies a new hire's ID documents before creating their account. What is this?
questions.explain: Proofing confirms the person is who they say they are.

questions.q: A long passphrase is generally stronger than a short complex password.
questions.explain: Length adds far more possible combinations than symbol rules.

questions.q: When an employee leaves, their account should be disabled as part of deprovisioning.
questions.explain: Prompt deprovisioning stops former staff from using old access.

questions.q: Match the access model to its description.
pairs: Rights based on system rules such as ACLs
questions.explain: Access model questions are very common.

questions.explain: PAM vaults hold privileged credentials and rotate them.

questions.q: Match the authentication factor to the example.
questions.explain: MFA needs two or more different factor types.

learn.idea: Scripts and orchestration do repetitive security work quickly and the same way every time. They need care so mistakes do not spread fast.
points: Use cases: user and resource provisioning, guard rails, security groups, ticket creation, escalation, enabling and disabling services, CI testing, integrations and APIs.
Benefits: efficiency, enforced baselines, standard infrastructure, scaling securely, staff retention, faster reaction, workforce multiplier.
Considerations: complexity, cost, single point of failure, technical debt, ongoing supportability.
SOAR (security orchestration, automation and response) runs playbooks that tie tools together.
learn.memory: Automate the boring, review the dangerous.

cards.back: Runs automated playbooks across security tools.
Automated limits that stop unsafe changes.
Automation lets a small team do more.
Shortcuts that cost more to fix later.
Automated tests each time code is merged.
A bad script can make mistakes at scale.

questions.q: When a phishing email is reported, a system automatically pulls it from every inbox, blocks the sender and opens a ticket. What is this?
questions.explain: SOAR orchestrates tools to respond in seconds.

questions.q: A cloud policy automatically blocks anyone from creating a public storage bucket. What is this?
questions.explain: Guard rails enforce secure settings automatically.

questions.q: Which is a risk of heavy automation?
options: A faulty script can make the same mistake across thousands of systems
It always lowers staff skills to zero
It removes the need for logging
questions.explain: Automation multiplies errors as well as good work, so test and review it.

questions.q: A new hire's accounts, groups and laptop are set up automatically from the HR record. Which use case is this?
questions.explain: Automated provisioning is fast and consistent.

questions.q: Which benefit of automation helps a small security team handle the work of a much larger one?
questions.explain: Automation multiplies what each analyst can do.

questions.q: Old, poorly documented automation scripts can become technical debt.
questions.explain: Scripts that nobody understands are hard to support and risky to change.

questions.q: Match the consideration to its meaning.
pairs: More moving parts that can break
One automation outage stops many tasks
Someone must maintain it long term
questions.explain: These weigh against the benefits.

learn.idea: When an incident happens, a planned process limits damage. Forensics preserves evidence so findings stand up later.
points: Process: preparation, detection, analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned.
Training and testing: tabletop exercises and simulations.
Root cause analysis finds why it happened. Threat hunting looks for attackers who slipped past alerts.
Forensics: legal hold, chain of custody, acquisition, reporting, preservation, e-discovery.

Order of volatility: collect the most volatile first: CPU registers and cache, then routing and ARP tables, process table and live connections, then RAM, temporary files and swap, disk, remote logs, and finally backups and archives.
Hash evidence images so you can prove they have not changed.

Eradication.
Record of who handled evidence, when and why.
Order to keep relevant data and stop deleting it.
CPU registers and cache, then RAM.
Review after an incident to improve.

Metadata such as email headers, file timestamps and photo EXIF data can reveal who, when and where.
Packet captures show full content but take lots of storage. Flow data shows who talked to whom with less detail.

learn.idea: Governance sets the rules and who is responsible. Policies say what must happen, standards set the specifics, and procedures say how.
points: Policies: acceptable use (AUP), information security, business continuity, disaster recovery, incident response, SDLC, change management.
Standards: password, access control, physical security, encryption. Procedures: step-by-step instructions such as onboarding, offboarding and playbooks. Guidelines are recommendations, not rules.
External considerations: regulatory, legal, industry, local, regional, national and global.
Governance structures: boards, committees, government entities, centralised or decentralised.

Data roles: owner (accountable, sets classification), controller (decides why and how personal data is processed), processor (processes data for the controller), custodian or steward (looks after data day to day).
learn.memory: Policy = what. Standard = exactly what. Procedure = how. Guideline = should.

Recommended practice, not mandatory.

Processes data on behalf of the controller.
Handles day-to-day care of data, such as backups.
Step-by-step procedure for a specific incident type.

questions.explain: Standards give specific, measurable requirements that support a policy.

questions.q: A step-by-step checklist explains how to disable a leaving employee's accounts and collect their laptop. What is this?
questions.explain: Procedures describe exactly how to carry out a task.

questions.explain: Custodians implement and maintain protections.

questions.explain: Guidelines are best-practice advice, not mandatory rules.

questions.explain: Playbooks are procedures for specific incident types.

questions.explain: The software development life cycle policy builds security into each stage.

learn.idea: Risk management finds risks, measures them and chooses how to treat each one. Quantitative analysis puts money figures on risk.
points: SLE (single loss expectancy) = asset value x exposure factor. ALE (annualised loss expectancy) = SLE x ARO (annualised rate of occurrence).
Qualitative analysis uses ratings such as high, medium and low. Quantitative uses numbers.
Assessments can be ad hoc, recurring, one-time or continuous.

Risk register: risks, key risk indicators, owners and thresholds. Risk appetite is how much risk the organisation will take on (expansionary, conservative, neutral). Risk tolerance is how much variation it will accept.
Strategies: transfer (insurance), accept (including exemptions and exceptions), avoid (stop the activity), mitigate (reduce it).
Business impact analysis (BIA) sets RTO, RPO, MTTR and MTBF for critical functions.
learn.memory: SLE = AV x EF. ALE = SLE x ARO.

cards.back: Asset value x exposure factor.
SLE x ARO.
Cyber insurance.
Stopping the risky activity altogether.
Document listing risks, owners, ratings and responses.
Amount of risk an organisation is willing to pursue.

questions.q: A server is worth $40,000. A flood would destroy 25% of its value. What is the single loss expectancy?

questions.q: The SLE for a laptop theft is $2,500 and the company expects 6 thefts a year. What is the ALE?

questions.q: A company stops selling a product in a country because the data laws there are too risky. Which strategy is this?
questions.explain: Avoidance removes the activity that creates the risk.

learn.idea: Vendors and suppliers can bring risk into your organisation. Assess them before signing and keep watching after.
points: Vendor assessment: penetration testing, right-to-audit clause, evidence of internal audits, independent assessments, supply chain analysis.
Vendor selection: due diligence, checking for conflicts of interest.

Agreements: SLA (service levels), MOA (memorandum of agreement), MOU (memorandum of understanding), MSA (master service agreement), SOW or work order (specific work), NDA (confidentiality), BPA (business partners agreement).
Ongoing vendor monitoring, security questionnaires and rules of engagement for any testing.
learn.memory: MSA sets the terms once. Each SOW says what this job is.

cards.back: Lets you audit the vendor's controls.
Master agreement covering general terms for future work.
Statement of work describing a specific project.
Business partners agreement covering a partnership.
Investigating a vendor before signing.
Agreed limits and scope for a security test.

questions.q: A contract clause lets the customer inspect the cloud provider's security controls. What is it?
questions.explain: Right-to-audit gives the customer the ability to check controls.

questions.q: A company signs one agreement with an IT firm covering general terms, then signs a separate document for each project. What is that separate document?
questions.explain: The MSA holds standing terms. Each SOW describes specific work, deliverables and timelines.

questions.q: Before choosing a payroll provider, the company checks its financial health, breach history and certifications. What is this?
questions.explain: Due diligence is research before you commit.

questions.q: Which document sets out the scope, timing and limits for a penetration test of a vendor's systems?
questions.explain: Rules of engagement prevent testing from going outside agreed bounds.

questions.q: The security team sends a vendor a list of questions about encryption, access control and incident response. What is this?
questions.explain: Questionnaires collect information about a vendor's controls.

questions.q: A procurement manager owns shares in a vendor bidding for a contract. What must be checked?
questions.explain: Conflicts of interest can bias vendor selection.

questions.q: Which document sets the measurable uptime and response times a vendor must meet?
questions.explain: A service level agreement defines performance targets.

questions.q: An MOU is usually less formal and less binding than a contract.
questions.explain: An MOU states shared intent. An MOA is usually more specific.

questions.q: Once a vendor is approved there is no need to monitor them again.
questions.explain: Vendor risk changes, so ongoing monitoring is needed.

questions.q: Match the agreement to its purpose.
pairs: General terms for an ongoing relationship
questions.explain: Agreement types are tested in this domain.

learn.idea: Compliance means meeting laws, regulations and contracts. Privacy laws give people rights over their personal data.
points: Reporting can be internal or external. Consequences of non-compliance: fines, sanctions, reputational damage, loss of licence, contractual impacts.
Compliance monitoring: due diligence and due care, attestation and acknowledgement, internal and external checks, automation.
Privacy: local, regional, national and global laws. The data subject is the person the data is about.
Controller vs processor, data ownership, data inventory and retention, and the right to be forgotten (erasure under GDPR).
learn.memory: Due diligence is checking. Due care is doing.

cards.back: The person the personal data is about.
A person's right to have their data erased.
Taking reasonable action to protect assets.
Investigating and understanding risks.
Fines, sanctions, reputational damage or loss of licence.
Formal statement that controls are in place.

questions.q: A customer asks a European company to delete all personal data it holds about them. Which right are they using?
questions.explain: GDPR gives data subjects the right to erasure in many cases.

questions.q: Under privacy law, what is the person whose personal data is collected called?
questions.explain: The data subject is the individual the data describes.

questions.q: A company is fined and loses its ability to process card payments after failing a PCI DSS audit. What are these?
questions.explain: Fines, sanctions and loss of licence are typical consequences.

questions.q: Management patches systems promptly and trains staff, doing what a reasonable company would do. What principle is this?
questions.explain: Due care is acting responsibly. Due diligence is the research and checking that informs it.

questions.q: Each employee signs a form every year confirming they have read the security policy. What is this?
questions.explain: Acknowledgement records that staff were informed.

questions.q: Keeping personal data longer than needed can itself be a compliance problem.
questions.explain: Retention limits are part of privacy law. Keep data only as long as required.

questions.q: Match the privacy term to its meaning.
pairs: List of what personal data you hold and where
questions.explain: Privacy programmes start with knowing what data you have.

questions.q: A company uses software that continuously checks cloud settings against PCI DSS rules and reports drift. What is this?
questions.explain: Automation keeps compliance checks continuous rather than yearly.

learn.idea: Audits check that controls exist and work. Penetration tests try to break in to show what an attacker could really do.
points: Internal audits and self-assessments, often reporting to an audit committee. External: regulatory examinations, independent third-party audits.
Penetration testing types: physical, offensive (red team), defensive (blue team), integrated (purple team).
Environment knowledge: known (white box, full details), partially known (grey box), unknown (black box, no details).
Reconnaissance: passive (public information, no contact with the target) and active (scanning and probing the target).
learn.memory: Known, partially known, unknown: how much the tester is told up front.

cards.back: Tester gets no prior information.
Tester gets full details such as diagrams and code.
Gathering public info without touching the target.
Scanning or probing the target directly.
Offensive attackers in an exercise.
Red and blue working together to improve defences.

questions.q: A tester is given network diagrams, source code and admin accounts before starting. Which type of test is this?
questions.explain: Full information is a known environment (white box) test.

questions.q: A tester is only given the company name and must find everything else. Which type of test is this?
questions.explain: No prior information is an unknown environment (black box) test.

questions.q: A tester reads the company's job adverts, LinkedIn pages and DNS records without touching its systems. What is this?
questions.explain: Passive recon uses public sources with no direct contact.

questions.q: A tester runs Nmap against the company's public IP range. What is this?
questions.explain: Scanning sends traffic to the target, so it is active.

questions.q: Attackers and defenders share findings live during an exercise to improve detection. What is this called?
questions.explain: Purple teaming combines red and blue to build better defences.

questions.q: A government regulator reviews a bank's security controls. What type of audit is this?
questions.explain: Regulators examine regulated firms from outside.

questions.q: A physical penetration test might include trying to tailgate into a building.
questions.explain: Physical tests check doors, badges, guards and staff awareness.

questions.q: Match the team to its role.
questions.explain: Team colours are used in exercise questions.

learn.idea: People are a strong defence when they know what to look for and how to report it. Awareness programmes train, test and measure.
points: Phishing campaigns test whether staff recognise and report phishing.
Recognising anomalous behaviour: risky, unexpected or unintentional actions.

User guidance and training: policies and handbooks, situational awareness, insider threat, password management, removable media and cables, social engineering, operational security, hybrid and remote work.
Reporting and monitoring: initial and recurring. Programmes need development and execution.
learn.memory: See something odd, report it, even if you clicked.

cards.back: Fake phishing emails sent to test and train staff.
Not leaking useful details, such as on social media.
Threats change and people forget.
Home networks and public Wi-Fi are less controlled.
Mistakes such as sending data to the wrong person.
Report rate and click rate.

questions.q: The security team sends fake phishing emails and gives instant training to anyone who clicks. What is this?
questions.explain: Simulations measure and improve how staff handle phishing.

questions.q: An employee posts a photo of their desk on social media showing a whiteboard with server names and passwords. Which training topic would help?
questions.explain: OPSEC teaches staff not to leak sensitive details.

questions.q: A user accidentally emails a customer list to the wrong external address. What kind of behaviour is this?
questions.explain: It was a mistake, not an attack, but it still needs reporting and response.

questions.q: Security awareness training only needs to be given once, when staff are hired.
questions.explain: Recurring training keeps people up to date with new threats.

questions.q: Which metric best shows a phishing programme is working over time?
options: More users reporting simulated phishing and fewer clicking
Fewer help desk tickets for printers
Higher CPU on the mail server
questions.explain: Rising report rates and falling click rates show real behaviour change.
